data.title: AI selloff: Taiwan's benchmark index posts worst week since 1991
data.description:
Taiwan's stock market extended losses on Friday, capping off its worst week in decades, tracking the global tech selloff as Anthropic's (ANT) IPO failed to quell concerns over the AI trade.

The tech-heavy TAIEX Index (TWSE) closed down 6.6% on Friday. It ended the week 17.5% lower, notching its worst week since 1991.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM), which accounts for over 40% of TAIEX's weighting, slid nearly 5%.

Anthopic (ANT) made its record stock market debut on Thursday, and while shares initially soared amid opening-day euphoria, they pared gains later in the session. The stock is down 6% premarket on Friday.

"The message is becoming clearer: investors still believe in AI's potential, but are increasingly questioning how much they should pay for that potential," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist, Saxo.

Anthropic's (ANT) IPO "arrives at a moment when strong AI earnings and fundraising announcements are no longer enough to lift the entire sector," she added.

Recent tech outages and Nvidia's (NVDA) leadership turmoil had already dented sentiment prior to Anthropic's (ANT) IPO.

TAIEX (TWSE) also saw a steep selloff on Monday, when the index fell 6%. Barclays said the rout was primarily driven by forced selling by retail investors.

While Taiwan's market regulator recently tightened curbs on short selling, the move hasn't done much to help stabilize the market.

"Limiting short-selling activity does not eliminate underlying bearish sentiment or selling pressure from investors reducing existing long exposure," Matthew Unterman, head of research at S3 Partners, told Bloomberg News.

data.title: Trump administration signed off nearly 900,000 Nvidia, AMD AI chips for China in six months
Biggest stock movers Friday: ANT, INTU, and more
data.description:
Stock futures edged lower Friday morning as Anthropic's record-breaking IPO failed to ease broader valuation and rate-hike fears weighing on the AI trade. 

Here are some of Friday's biggest stock movers:

Biggest stock gainers

  • Gap (GAP) +3% - Shares rose after the retailer reported mixed Q3 results, with adjusted EPS of $0.82 beating the $0.78 consensus and comparable sales outperforming expectations at Old Navy and Gap, offsetting continued weakness at Athleta and Banana Republic. Comparable sales declined 15% at Athleta and 3% at Banana Republic, missing expectations for declines of 11% and growth of 2.45%, respectively. GAAP EPS increased 39% to $0.86, helped by IEEPA tariff refunds, which also supported operating margin expansion to 9.9% from a year earlier. However, Gap lowered its FY2026 outlook, now expecting adjusted EPS of $2.29–$2.34 vs. its prior $2.35–$2.45 range and the $2.40 consensus, while forecasting flat net sales of approximately $15.4B. The company also named Ashley Kechter, formerly global president of Vuori and Fabletics, as Athleta's new president and CEO, effective December 14.

Biggest stock losers

  • Intuit (INTU) -10% - Shares plunged despite FQ1 results topping expectations, as the fintech lowered its full-year revenue outlook on weaker-than-expected Credit Karma growth and issued a softer-than-anticipated Q2 forecast. Non-GAAP EPS rose 56% Y/Y to $2.91, beating the $2.64 consensus, while revenue increased 12% to $4.4B, above the $4.31B estimate. However, Intuit cut its FY2027 revenue outlook from $23.28B–$23.51B previously to $23.08B–$23.37B, citing slower consumer demand and revised Credit Karma growth expectations of 3%–7%, down from 11%–13%, while maintaining its adjusted EPS outlook of $22.88–$23.12. Q2 revenue is forecast at $4.93B–$4.95B, below the $5.11B consensus, while adjusted EPS guidance of $3.17–$3.22 also fell short of the $3.73 estimate. Separately, Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68B, comprising $3.31B in cash and $368M in stock, with the transaction expected to close in early 2027.
  • Anthropic (ANT) -6% - Shares fell for a second consecutive trading session as a broader market selloff and concerns over AI-sector valuations weighed on sentiment following the company’s record-setting IPO. The stock dropped to $91.25 in early trading, compared with Thursday’s close of $97.17, but remained above its $83 IPO price after jumping 17% in its debut. Anthropic’s $107.3B IPO attracted demand for seven times the shares on offer, with more than half of institutional investors reportedly receiving no allocation, underscoring the strong investor appetite behind its debut.

data.title: Guardforce AI to implement 1-for-40 reverse share split
data.description:
Guardforce AI (GFAI) said it will implement a 1-for-40 reverse share split, with its Class A ordinary shares expected to begin trading on a split-adjusted basis on the Nasdaq Capital Market at the open on Nov. 24.

The reverse split will reduce the number of issued and outstanding ordinary shares from ~31.9M to ~799,233, subject to adjustment for the rounding up of fractional entitlements described below.

The split, approved by the company's board and shareholders, became effective Nov. 11 following registration with the Cayman Islands Registrar of Companies. The company also completed a related capital reduction, share subdivision, and re-designation of its share capital into Class A and Class B ordinary shares.

The Class A shares will replace the existing ordinary shares, continue trading under the “GFAI” ticker.

GFAI shares fell 7.5% premarket.

data.title: U.S. stock futures move lower as Anthropic debut fails to revive AI trade
data.description:
U.S. stock futures fell early Friday as investors assessed the fallout from Wall Street's sharp selloff in the previous session, when major indexes tumbled more than 2% each. 

Sentiment toward artificial intelligence stocks remained under pressure after Anthropic's much-anticipated public market debut failed to provide the boost investors had hoped for, extending a volatile week for equities.

Nasdaq 100 futures (US100:IND) fell 0.85% while S&P 500 futures (SPX) slipped 0.33%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures (INDU) edged lower 0.01%.

Anthropic's (ANT) historic Nasdaq debut on Thursday marked the first pure-play AI lab to go public. Shares opened at $111.50, 33% above the IPO price of $83, before retreating to close at $96.97. Despite the scale of the debut, the stock's retreat from its opening price failed to provide the broader AI trade with a sustained boost. ANT shares are down 6% premarket.

U.S. Treasury yields moved lower across the curve. The 2-year Treasury yield (US2Y) fell 4.1 basis points to 4.73%, while the 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) dropped 3.8 basis points to 5.01%. The 30-year Treasury yield (US30Y) declined 3.1 basis points to 5.38%.

Investors will look to the final February reading of the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index for fresh signals on the economy. BJ's Wholesale is also scheduled to report quarterly results before the opening bell.

Top S&P 500 gainers included CBRE (CBRE) +8.32%, KKR (KKR) +5.65%, and Aon (AON) +2.00%. Decliners included Ross Stores (ROST) -4.74%, Solventum (SOLV) -4.32%, and West Pharmaceutical Services (WST) -2.44%.

data.title: Anthropic shares slip after rallying in record-breaking IPO debut
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) shares fell in their second day of trading as a broader market selloff and growing concerns over the AI trade weighed on sentiment following the stock’s record-setting debut.

The company’s shares fell as much as 7.4% in early premarket trading Friday, a day after surging 17% in their public market debut. The stock traded as low as $90 as of 4:02 a.m. in New York, compared with Thursday's closing price of $97.17. Shares remained above the IPO price of $83.

The decline came amid broader market weakness, with Nasdaq 100 futures down 0.9%. The initial surge reflected strong investor demand for the heavily oversubscribed IPO, but the company's steep valuation and fresh competitive threats weighed on shares Friday as investors broadly pulled back from riskier assets.

Anthropic’s $107.3B IPO attracted global demand for seven times the shares on offer. Competition was so intense that more than half of institutional investors bidding for shares received no allocation, Bloomberg reported Thursday. The IPO surpassed the previous record set by SpaceX (SPCX) in June, which raised a total of $86.25B, including additional shares sold by underwriters through the overallotment option.

Goldman Sachs Group (GS), Morgan Stanley (MS), and 20 other banks earned a record $550M in fees for their work on Anthropic’s IPO.

data.title: Clearsign outlines path to breakeven at 160 burners per year as texas 26-burner startup nears completion
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: ClearSign Technologies Corporation (CLIR) Q3 2026

Management view

  • CEO Colin James Deller framed ClearSign’s value proposition around avoiding add-on emissions controls: “With our unique technology, we can provide special burners that essentially do not make the NOx emissions in the first place.” He added a specific customer comparison: “their estimate to put an SCR and solve their problem that way was $15 million. Using the ClearSign burners, we believe their total cost to be in the region of $5 to $10 million.”

  • On the 26-burner Gulf Coast petrochemical installation, CEO Deller said, “It’s going great,” adding that installation “went absolutely smoothly” and “I believe we’re ahead of schedule… we’ll be done within about a week.” He also described the external validation mechanism: “the data from those emissions monitors will be the metric… everyone’s looking forward to for the technical success of this installation.”

  • On leverage from the startup, CEO Deller said, “I personally will be making phone calls to those people explaining what we’ve done, trying to talk them to come and see it,” and later reinforced the expected impact: “We believe so… they are waiting to see the technology running in somebody else’s heater.”

  • CFO Brent Hinds reported Q3 revenue and margin dynamics: “the company recognized approximately $712,000 in revenues,” and “Our third quarter gross profit margin was approximately 55.6%,” attributing the margin lift to “a licensing arrangement with an OEM heater manufacturer.”

Outlook

  • Management did not issue formal revenue or EPS guidance, and Investor Relations stated: “Any estimates we discuss today regarding our pipeline or potential future orders are forward-looking statements and are not guidance.”

  • For the newly announced DOE program with Kern Energy, CEO Deller described timing expectations with permitting caveats: “My expectations are that we will receive the order from them early Q1… I do believe that they’re still completing permits,” and “my best guess will be to complete the order somewhere around late Q3, early Q4 next year.”

  • For M Series momentum, CEO Deller said, “I am expecting additional orders for M Series burners before the year is out,” while emphasizing limited visibility: “I can’t make any guarantees.”

Financial results

  • CFO Hinds reported Q3 revenue of “approximately $712,000” vs. “approximately $1 million” in the prior-year period, and said the year-over-year decrease was “primarily attributable to product mix,” while the same mix “generated meaningful improvement in gross margins.”

  • CFO Hinds reported gross margin of “approximately 55.6%” vs. “35.8%” in the prior-year period, and tied the change to licensing: “primarily driven by our licensing arrangement with an OEM heater manufacturer.” He also stated a long-term target: “help us achieve our overall long-term company gross margin target of 40%.”

  • CFO Hinds said Q3 net loss “decreased by $361,000” year over year, driven by “a $601,000 decrease in general and administrative expenses,” partially offset by “a $233,000 decrease in other income,” adding that “our Department of Energy grant completed in May of 2026.”

  • On liquidity, CFO Hinds said: “net cash used in operations… was approximately $1.3 million,” and cash and equivalents were “approximately $10.3 million” as of September 30, 2026, with “approximately 6.8 million shares of common stock outstanding.”

Q&A

  • Sameer Joshi, H.C. Wainwright: asked about gross margin and the “licensing arrangement”; CEO Deller answered, “we are able to provide the fabrication drawings to the client on a licensing basis,” and added, “For ClearSign, we make exactly the same profit, whether it’s a license sale or whether we are supplying the equipment.”

  • Sameer Joshi, H.C. Wainwright: asked if other customers may adopt licensing; CEO Deller said, “I’m absolutely open to that… though I’ve not had any other discussions… but we certainly expect more orders in this manner from this one customer.”

  • Sameer Joshi, H.C. Wainwright: asked about sequential OpEx decline; CFO Hinds said it was “driven by the vesting of restricted stock units, which were noncash, and legal expenses as well.”

  • Peter Gastreich, Water Tower Research: asked DOE/Kern opportunity size and timing; CEO Deller said it was “in the range of $500,000 to $750,000 from memory,” and reiterated expected ordering “early Q1” with completion “late Q3, early Q4 next year,” subject to permits.

  • Peter Gastreich, Water Tower Research: asked about yield/uplift beyond NOx compliance; CEO Deller said, “if we can improve the yield or improve the uptime… we actually give them a significant return on their investment,” and noted the Texas process-burner project on hold “was actually based on improving the uptime… as one of the primary drivers.”

  • Peter Gastreich, Water Tower Research: asked about CFD-to-field development and AI; CEO Deller said, “The ability to design a burner in CFD… is a game changer,” adding, “the very first M1 burner… that design has never been touched… demonstrated NOx down below 2 ppm.”

Sentiment analysis

  • Analyst tone was slightly positive and validation-seeking, with emphasis on unit economics, conversion, and funding-backed deployments, including “Can you explain that a little bit more?” (Joshi) and “Could you give us a sense of the size of the opportunity and roughly when the burners would go in?” (Gastreich).

  • Management tone was positive and catalyst-driven in both prepared discussion and Q&A, with repeated confidence signals around near-term operational proof points, including “It’s going great” (CEO Colin James Deller) and “I am expecting additional orders” (CEO Deller), while using caveats on timing such as “I can’t make any guarantees” (CEO Deller).

  • Versus Q2, management’s tone shifted from “scheduled to be in October” (Q2) toward imminent completion and reference-building, including “within about a week” (Q3), while analysts remained focused on commercialization mechanics (margins, order flow, program timing) across both calls.

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Q3 featured higher reported gross margin tied to a completed licensing/OEM delivery, while Q2 described margin as “approximately 41%” and characterized it as “relatively flat year-over-year.”

  • The 36-burner Texas process-burner delay description changed: Q2 attributed the hold to “delay in the client financing,” while Q3 said it was “due to internal organizational changes within the client” and added, “we also do not have any updates.”

  • Q2 emphasized balance sheet actions and governance, including “we raised additional funds… 500,000 shares… at $3.54 per share” and the Board addition of “Larry Saddler”; Q3 emphasized operational commissioning events (Texas 26-burner start-up; California flare start-up) and scaling mechanisms (licensing).

Risks and concerns

  • Investor Relations cautioned on commercialization timing and project execution: “timing of customer orders and our ability to convert proposals into orders,” “delays, holds or cancellations of customer projects,” and “our reliance on original equipment manufacturers and other third parties.”

  • Management highlighted permitting and schedule uncertainty for DOE/Kern: “they’re still completing permits,” and emphasized limited control over order timing, including “outside of our control” dynamics around customer schedules and purchase-order release.

Final takeaway

Management centered the quarter on imminent field validation and scaling channels: the Gulf Coast 26-burner startup was described as running ahead of schedule with CEMS emissions data positioned as the core proof point, licensing was credited with lifting Q3 gross margin to 55.6% while preserving “exactly the same profit,” and the DOE/Kern program was characterized as an expected early-Q1 order with completion targeted for late Q3 or early Q4 of next year, subject to permitting and customer timing.
